client: I've been struggling a lot since my mom passed away six months ago — it was so sudden, and I honestly still can't believe she's gone. The hardest part lately is that my friends all seem to have just... moved on with their lives, like everything is normal, and I feel completely alone in still grieving. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — losing your mom so suddenly, and then feeling like the world around you just kept moving while you're still standing in that moment of loss. That sense of being alone in your grief, like no one else is holding space for it anymore, can feel almost like a second loss. I'm really glad you decided to try talking about it, and I want you to know this is a place where there's no timeline on grief — we can go at whatever pace feels right for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, "second loss" is actually a really accurate way to put it — I hadn't thought of it like that before, but that's exactly what it feels like. Like I lost my mom, and then I also lost this sense that the people around me actually get what I'm going through. I guess part of me is still a little skeptical that talking about it here will help, because I've tried opening up to a couple of friends and it just felt awkward and like they didn't really know what to say.
therapist: It makes a lot of sense that you'd feel skeptical here — when you've reached out and been met with awkwardness or silence, it teaches you to expect that reaching out won't feel safe or worth it. That's a really understandable way to protect yourself. I'm curious, when those moments with friends felt awkward, what did you find yourself wishing they had said or done differently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think I just wanted them to sit with it a little longer instead of immediately trying to make me feel better or change the subject. Like, one friend kept saying things like "she's in a better place" or "at least you have good memories," and while I know she meant well, it just felt like she was trying to wrap it up in a bow so we could move on. I didn't need solutions — I just wanted someone to acknowledge that this is really, really hard and that it's okay that I'm still not okay.
therapist: What you just described — wanting someone to simply *sit* in the hard place with you rather than rush to fix it — is such a profound and valid need, and it sounds like you've actually just done that for yourself right now by naming it so clearly. That phrase, "it's okay that I'm still not okay," is really important, and I want you to know that's exactly the kind of space I want this to be for you. Can you tell me a little more about what "still not okay" looks like for you day to day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Day to day it's kind of like... I'll be fine for a few hours, just going through the motions at work or whatever, and then something completely random will set me off — like seeing a certain brand of tea she used to drink, or hearing a song she liked. And then I feel this wave of guilt on top of the grief, because sometimes I catch myself laughing at something or having a good moment, and it feels almost wrong, like I'm somehow betraying her by not being sad every second. It's exhausting to feel like I can't win either way — sad when I'm sad, and guilty when I'm not.
therapist: What you're describing — that impossible double bind of grief and guilt — is one of the most exhausting parts of loss, and it makes complete sense that it's wearing you down. I notice that even as you're describing something so painful, there's something almost quiet and careful in the way you're sharing it, like maybe you're holding a lot more than what's making it into words right now. Is there something underneath all of this that feels even harder to say out loud?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: There is something, yeah, but it's hard to even admit because it makes me feel like a terrible person. The last time I talked to my mom, we had kind of a stupid argument — nothing major, just one of those pointless disagreements — and I never got the chance to fix it before she died. I think underneath all the grief, what's really eating at me is that she might have died thinking I was angry with her, and I can't ever undo that.
therapist: First, I want to say clearly: what you just shared doesn't make you a terrible person — it makes you a deeply human one, because almost every relationship has unresolved moments, and the cruelty of sudden loss is that it takes away our chance to close them. What strikes me is that you carried this in for a while before saying it out loud just now, and I imagine it's been a heavy thing to hold alone. I'm wondering — if you could know what your mom was actually holding in her heart in those final days, what do you think she would have wanted you to know?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... I think she would have wanted me to know that she didn't even remember being upset by the time it happened, because that's just who she was — she never held grudges, not really. But even as I say that, there's this voice in my head that tells me I'm just making that up to make myself feel better, like I can't actually trust that thought because I want it to be true so badly. It's hard to know how to hold onto something that feels comforting when part of me is convinced I'm only believing it out of desperation.
therapist: What you just described about your mom — that she wasn't someone who held onto hurt — that didn't sound like desperation to me; it sounded like you genuinely *knowing* her, the way only someone who loved her closely could. That critical voice that tells you you can't trust your own knowledge of the person you knew best is worth paying attention to, because it seems like it might be working very hard to block you from something that's actually true. What do you think it would mean for you — not just to think it, but to really let yourself believe that she wasn't holding that argument against you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I think it would mean I could actually let myself grieve her without this constant layer of shame on top of it, which honestly sounds like such a relief that it almost scares me. But I don't know how to just... decide to believe something, you know? Like you can't just flip a switch on a thought that's been eating at you for six months. I want to believe it, I really do, but I'm not sure wanting it is enough to make it feel real.
therapist: You're so right that belief isn't a switch — it's more like something you build slowly through evidence and experience, and that's actually exactly the kind of work we can do together. But I want to gently stay with what you said, that the relief almost *scares* you — because that's a really important thing you named, and I don't want it to slip by. What do you think feels scary about the possibility of putting that shame down?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of what scares me is that the shame has kind of become the way I stay connected to her, like as long as I'm punishing myself over that argument, I'm still in some kind of conversation with her about it. If I let it go, it almost feels like I'm closing a door, and I'm terrified that once I stop holding onto the guilt, I'll just have to fully face the fact that she's gone and there's nothing left to resolve. It sounds strange when I say it out loud, but the guilt has almost been easier to live with than the finality of just... accepting the loss.
therapist: What you just said doesn't sound strange at all — it sounds like one of the most honest and courageous things you've said today, and I think you've just uncovered something really important about what the guilt has actually been *doing* for you. Letting go of it isn't betrayal or closing a door; it's actually the beginning of a different kind of connection with her — one built on who she really was, not on an argument she'd already forgiven. I'm wondering, what are some of the ways you might want to stay connected to her that don't require you to keep hurting yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That question actually caught me off guard a little, because I've been so focused on the guilt that I haven't really let myself think about what a gentler kind of connection to her could even look like. The first thing that came to mind was making that tea she used to drink — the one that always makes me cry when I see it in the store — but actually making it on purpose, like as a way of being with her rather than just being ambushed by the grief. I don't know, it feels a little small or maybe too simple compared to everything I've been carrying, but maybe that's okay?
therapist: That idea about the tea is not small at all — it's actually quite beautiful, because it takes something that's been ambushing you with pain and transforms it into something intentional and loving, which is a really meaningful shift. I notice there's something almost tentative in the way you offered it, like you're waiting for permission to trust your own instinct here. What would it feel like to try it this week, and let it be exactly as simple as it is?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I want to try it, I really do, but I'm also a little worried that I'll sit down with the tea and just completely fall apart, and then I'll be alone with all of that with no one there to help me through it. I live alone, and that's kind of the thing that makes a lot of these moments harder — there's no one to just be present with me when the grief hits. I guess I'm scared of intentionally walking toward something painful when I've been trying so hard just to hold myself together enough to get through each day.
therapist: The fear you're describing — of intentionally opening a door to pain when you're already working so hard just to stay upright — is completely understandable, and it takes real courage to even consider it. I also hear something important underneath what you're saying: that one of the deepest wounds right now isn't just the grief itself, but the aloneness of it, the fact that there's no one physically there to sit with you in those moments. What if we thought about the tea not as something you have to do alone in silence, but as something you could do while you're connected to support — even something like bringing it here, to one of our sessions, so you're not walking toward it completely by yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
